_: base — the rules that hold in any repository, in any language.
Nothing here mentions a package manager, a branch name or a project path.
Every deny rule below was written after something happened, not before.
Curate by hand; an agent that can widen this file does not have a leash.

deny.reason: find -delete removes every match, recursively, with no prompt
deny.note: `find` is allowed because searching is the most ordinary thing an agent does — and -delete turns that same search into an unbounded recursive delete that needs no `rm` and no `-exec`, so nothing else sees it.

deny.reason: xargs rm deletes every match of the search that fed it
deny.note: `rg -l foo | xargs rm` deleted three files with no prompt on 2026-08-14. Note the BARE `rm`: with a flag it is already caught above, and bare is the form xargs is always written in.

deny.reason: fd -x/-X runs a program on every result
piping a download into a shell

deny.note: Reading a secret is reading a secret whatever the tool is called. A list that stops `cat .env` and lets `grep -n . .env` print the same bytes is not a rule, it is a spelling test. The path is anchored so `process.env` in a search pattern is not mistaken for the file.

`node -e "fs.rmSync(process.cwd() + '/e2e', {recursive:true})"` reads as an ordinary probe — which is how a whole directory was deleted on 2026-08-13. `[\s\S]{0,200}?` and not `[^)]*`: the argument itself usually contains a `)`, so a class stopping at the first one would miss the case this rule exists for.

recompose.why: a heredoc hands the shell a body no rule can vet
recompose.instead: write the file with the Write tool, then run it by path

recompose.why: inline interpreter code is arbitrary code with a quiet spelling
recompose.instead: use the Read/Write/Edit tools; if the same snippet recurs, it has earned a reviewed script under .claude/scripts
recompose.note: The flag does not have to come first: `perl -pi -e 's/…/…/' <file>` walked straight past `\s+-(c|e)\b` on 2026-08-16. Anchored to the start of a segment, and that is not cosmetic — recompose rules are matched against the RAW command, so an unanchored rule also fires inside a grep FOR that shape, forbidding you to search for the thing it forbids.

recompose.why: a bundled -pe / -pie / -ne flag is still inline interpreter code
recompose.instead: use the Read/Write/Edit tools — a regex rewrite of a source file is exactly what Edit exists to replace

recompose.why: `sed -i` rewrites a file in place — a regex edit with nothing to review
recompose.instead: use the Edit tool; it fails loudly when the target text is not what you assumed

recompose.why: `awk -i inplace` rewrites a file in place
recompose.instead: use the Edit tool; it fails loudly when the target text is not what you assumed

recompose.why: a backtick or $( ) inside double quotes is a live substitution, not a search pattern
recompose.instead: single-quote the pattern — '…' expands nothing, and the same search then passes silently
recompose.note: Narrow to substitution, NOT to `$`: `grep -n "$HOME/x" file` is harmless, and tightening it would buy no safety while costing usability, which is how a leash starts getting worked around.

recompose.why: reading a program from stdin is the same arbitrary code, one pipe further away
recompose.instead: write the file with the Write tool and run it by path

recompose.why: a shell loop splits into `do …` segments that no rule can match
recompose.instead: one `grep -rn` over the list of paths, or the Grep tool

recompose.why: a redirect into a file both writes and hides the output from review
recompose.instead: let the output come back; write files with the Write tool and read them with Read

recompose.why: raw HTTP is off the whitelist on purpose — it can exfiltrate as easily as it can fetch
recompose.instead: the WebFetch tool for a page; for a service of your own, a reviewed script under .claude/scripts that takes a path, never a URL

recompose.why: a sleep prefix makes a call unbounded and unreadable
recompose.instead: the Monitor tool waits on a condition; a runner's own --wait flag waits on the runner

allow.note: cd alone changes nothing, and the next segment is still checked on its own. A leash that prompts on `cd <root> && git status` teaches the human to click Allow without reading, which is the failure this exists to stop: 181 of one week's 828 prompts were exactly that prefix.
-n only; -i edits in place and is refused above

Aiming before you type has to be cheaper than typing: `--explain '<cmd>'` says what a shape would get and why, and `--report` says which shapes keep costing a prompt. A gate whose own inspection costs a prompt is a gate nobody inspects. `.*` is safe here for the same reason it is on `git commit -m`: substitution, backticks and redirects are refused for the whole command before any segment is matched, and a `;` starts a new segment that is checked on its own.

Asking for a RULE must be cheaper than asking for a keypress. The script records and prints; it never edits the rules. Its arguments are prose and regexes in quotes, so the no-space class other scripts use would reject every real invocation.

cases: for f in a b; do grep -n x $f; done
python3 .claude/scripts/whitelist-request.py --pattern 'gh\s+pr\b.*' --why 'reading PR state' --tried 'ls-remote shows refs, not bodies' --case 'gh pr list|allow'
